S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.

subtypes.Initial Insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep and taking a long time to do so.
subtypes.Middle Insomnia: Waking up frequently during sleep or having difficulty falling back asleep.
subtypes.Early Morning Awakening: Waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep.
subtypes.Hypersomnia: Sleeping for long periods at night or excessive sleep during the day.
subtypes.Nightmare Disorder: Sleep disturbance caused by repeated and distressing dreams.
subtypes.Non-Restorative Sleep: Feeling unrefreshed despite having slept enough.

S029.name: Fatigue
S029.description: Persistent fatigue that is not relieved by rest and a marked lack of energy.

subtypes.Chronic Fatigue: Fatigue that persists for a long period even after adequate rest.
subtypes.Physical Fatigue: A state of physical exhaustion where the body feels heavy and easily tires even from minor activities.
subtypes.Mental Fatigue: A state where fatigue accumulates rapidly during the process of thinking or concentrating.
subtypes.Loss of Energy: Difficulty performing daily activities due to a decline in energy and vitality.

S056.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
S056.description: Excessive anxiety and worry (expectant apprehension) occurring persistently about a number of events or activities.

subtypes.Chronic Worry: Worry occurs more days than not for at least 6 months.
subtypes.Generalized Worry: Worry is not confined to specific topics but spreads to various domains like work, school, family, and finances.
subtypes.Catastrophizing: Jumping to conclusions that minor mistakes or events will lead to irreversible disasters.
subtypes.Intolerance of Uncertainty: Unable to tolerate future uncertainty, trapped in 'what if' questions.

S057.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
S057.description: The subjective experience of finding it difficult to stop or control the worry.

subtypes.Failure to Control: Unable to regulate worry despite efforts to stop or distract oneself.
subtypes.Intrusive Worry: Worries suddenly intrude into the mind and interfere with focus while doing other tasks.
subtypes.Chaining of Worry: One worry triggers another in a chain reaction, escalating to catastrophic thoughts.

S059.name: Concentration_Difficulty
S059.description: Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank.

subtypes.Interference by Worry: Unable to focus on the task at hand because worries keep surfacing.
subtypes.Inability to Sustain Attention: Attention is scattered due to anxiety, making it hard to focus on one thing for long.
subtypes.Mind Going Blank: Suddenly the mind goes empty or white, and no thoughts occur.

symptom.disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive anxiety and worry about a variety of everyday events or activities, lasting for at least six months and often much longer. Individuals typically find it difficult to control the worry, which is accompanied by physical and cognitive manifestations such as restlessness, fatigue, concentration problems, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance. The course is often chronic and fluctuating, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to life stressors but a baseline tendency toward pervasive apprehension. GAD is distinguished from normal worry by its intensity, duration, and interference with functioning, and from other anxiety disorders by its broad, non–situation-specific focus rather than being tied to discrete fears or episodes.

patient.stressor: About a year and three months ago, Gregory’s store cut employee hours after a change in corporate management, and his schedule became irregular, with fluctuating shifts and reduced pay just as his wife’s hours at her job were also trimmed. The couple fell a month behind on a utility bill, and Gregory started picking up every extra shift offered, worrying constantly about keeping up with rent, car payments, and helping out his aging mother when unexpected expenses came up. Over the next year, the combination of unpredictable income, longer commutes for occasional side gigs, and his sense of responsibility to support both his household and church community slowly eroded the sense of ease he used to find in gardening, fishing, and volunteering. When he caught himself sitting at the register feeling utterly drained before his shift even started, dreading how he would make it through the day and still have energy for his family, his pastor encouraged him to talk to a doctor, and he was referred for psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “I feel worn out all the time no matter how much I rest, like I don’t have any energy left to get through work or take care of things at home.”
